claims.text: The starting coating is a nanoscale high-entropy-alloy multilayer containing mixed FCC and BCC crystal structures.
The starting multilayer exhibits inherent lattice distortion.
The starting multilayer has low initial strain-induced short-range order.
Sustained mechanical loading induces short-range order at the multilayer interfaces.
Newly formed interfacial short-range-ordered regions initially impede dislocation motion.
Continued loading causes the short-range-ordered regions to coarsen.
Coarsened short-range-ordered regions become channels that promote dislocation nucleation, cross-slip, and activation of additional slip systems.
The evolution of short-range order promotes deformation twinning under continued loading.
High internal stresses drive local atomic rearrangements that create interfacial short-range order.
Interfacial dislocation networks and twin boundaries become progressively activated during sustained loading.
The proposed evolution increases plastic deformation and ductility while preserving high strength.
Yield strength will decrease slightly relative to the pristine baseline.
Dislocation activity and twin density will increase relative to the pristine state.
The progressive deformation will be accompanied by work hardening.
Evolving interfacial short-range order should be detectable by in situ TEM or diffraction.
The mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact and catastrophic delamination or phase coarsening is absent.
Ambient or cryogenic conditions can be selected such that both dislocation slip and deformation twinning are active.
Loading conditions and local composition can alter the governing deformation response.
A controlled comparison between multilayers with different initial short-range order should reveal whether initial ordering affects progressive plastic deformation.
Failure to observe correlated short-range-order evolution and increased dislocation or twin activity, or failure of altered initial ordering to affect deformation, would falsify the hypothesis.
